description:
We are Think Tanks, a team of passionate and curious minds interested in technology, artificial intelligence, data science, and space exploration.

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are working on Dancing with the SARs, an interactive platform that uses NISAR satellite data to monitor and visualize changes on Earth's surface over time.
summary: NISAR Egypt Change Tracker is an open-source bilingual (English / العربية) web app that turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar into a 12-day picture of how Egypt’s surface actually changed from June to October 2026. We processed 40 real L2 GCOV passes over four landscapes: the Nile Delta, Fayoum Oasis, Toshka Lakes, and a Western Desert control site. The app lets anyone Know the season in numbers, See the dance on a map (animation, swipe, change masks), and Understand what the radar can and cannot claim. Every figure traces to a granule id. Water is backscatter-derived extent, not a flood map; causes stay hypotheses. The control site is the metronome: 0.0% changed pixels, and a reminder that dark sand can still look like water. This addresses “Dancing with the SARs” by making NISAR usable for water managers, farmers, New Valley planners, and classrooms when optical satellites fail in cloud, night, and dust.
details:
NISAR Egypt Change Tracker is a live, bilingual (English / العربية) web app that measures how Egypt’s surface changed from June to October 2026 using NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV radar. It does three things: Know the season in numbers, See the 12-day dance on a map, and Understand what the radar can and cannot claim.

How it works. We searched ASF for PROVISIONAL GCOV only (CRID P05023), streamed the needed HDF5 window over HTTPS, cropped each site, 4×4 multilooked, and wrote GeoTIFFs, PNG quicklooks, water and change masks, and a single labeled table. The web app reads that table — not an unconstrained model. Four sites, 40 real passes, one geometry and mode per site: Nile Delta, Fayoum Oasis, Toshka Lakes (mode 4005), and a Western Desert control (mode 2005). We never mix Toshka 4005 with 2005. The 27 Jul–10 Aug instrument gap is shown, never interpolated. Change uses a 3.0 dB threshold calibrated against a 0.37 dB desert noise floor. Water is a −18 dB backscatter class — extent, not flooding. Causes are hypotheses. Every number traces to a granule id. Ask NISAR answers only from the table and explainer; off-topic questions are refused; an optional Groq rephraser cannot invent a dB.

Benefits. Optical satellites fail in cloud, night, and dust. NISAR does not. A water manager, Delta farmer, New Valley planner, or teacher can open a phone or laptop every 12 days and see HH/HV, water-classified share, changed-pixel percent, and a before/after swipe — with the control site as the metronome (0.0% changed pixels, and a reminder that dark sand can still look like water: 29–43% on the control). Toshka’s 16–21% valid coverage is shown, not hidden. The 10 August Delta peak (32.55% changed pixels, HH −9.38 → −5.89 dB) is the seasonal story, not the quiet October pass.

Intended impact. Nile water and farmland feed a country that cannot walk every canal every fortnight. The project turns NISAR’s repeat cycle into a tool people in Egypt can actually use, and a classroom object that teaches radar without over-claiming floods. Live demo: https://nasa.notmohamedhany.me/

Tools and stack. Python 3.12 (numpy, h5py, rasterio) for the pipeline; React 18, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Recharts, i18next (RTL) for the app; nginx + HTTPS for deploy; optional Groq for phrasing only. No special hardware: a browser. Data: NASA–ISRO NISAR via ASF / Earthdata.

Creativity. The first screen is four real radar cards, not a menu. Know / See / Understand is a science story, not a dashboard dump. The Western Desert is a designed control, not a fourth pretty map. The assistant is constrained on purpose: refusing weather questions is a feature. Arabic is a first-class UI, not a translation overlay.

Factors we considered. Scientific honesty over a bigger claim (water ≠ flood; Toshka coverage caveat; no synthetic data). One mode per site even when another mode would look fuller. Calibration from a quiet desert, not a round number. Bilingual and mobile so the people the impact names can open it. NASA data as the engine: without the 40 granules there is no app.
